title: Settle the headless permission scope, then discover the six opening prompts by running them

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited abf97e2 (the merge of devteam2/sprint-12) from the main checkout at /Users/chrishobbs/Programming/fully-completely. Sprint file read fresh from main, including both post-creation amendments. Working tree clean apart from the known-inert .vscode/settings.json.

Neither FAIL trigger fired. This is the strongest evidence package this project has produced, and it is two things short of a PASS.

================================================================
THE TWO FAIL TRIGGERS — CHECKED FIRST, NEITHER FIRED
================================================================

REQ 3's trigger: "`npm publish` remaining an inference is a FAIL." It is not an inference. docs/sprint-12-permission-scope-findings.md records `npm publish --dry-run` run under exactly `--permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools "Bash(npm *)"` in a scratch package, succeeding with npm's own dry-run output and no permission block, plus a first attempt that npm itself refused on a prerelease-tag rule — which is npm validating, not a permission wall, and the distinction is drawn correctly. Both of Req 3's UNTESTED items were closed by running before Req 4 began, in the order Req 3 requires. Not a FAIL.

REQ 2's trigger: "an unrun scope claimed as working is a FAIL." I read the findings document hunting for exactly that and did not find one. Every mechanism claimed as working carries a described run: `acceptEdits` (with the surprising and useful detail that it blocks `npm --version` while allowing a real `git push` — a command-category classifier, not a network boundary), `--allowedTools "Bash(<pattern>)"` narrowing without leaking into adjacent categories, compound commands evaluated per sub-command, `--disallowedTools` returning "No such tool available" rather than a prompt. The four genuinely untested items are named as untested. The one hedged claim — the test-suite allowlist "CONFIRMED pattern... not yet run against the real command" — states its own gap rather than claiming coverage, and Req 4's Dev Team run subsequently exercised it for real. Not a FAIL.

BLANKET BYPASS IS ABSENT. Grepped the entire tree: `bypassPermissions` appears in exactly two places, both in launcher_test.js, in a test asserting it is never granted for any role. The refusal is enforced, not just recorded.

================================================================
REQ 4 — I DID NOT CLEAR THIS BY READING
================================================================

The criterion says this cannot be cleared by reading, and I caught desk-written templates in sprint 11 by cross-checking artifacts rather than by tone. Same method here.

THE CHECKABLE CLAIM, AND IT HOLDS. The discovery notes assert "the fixed scaffold and per-role pointers in scripts/launcher/prompts.js are UNCHANGED by this pass." The diffstat shows prompts.js changed by 62 lines, which is what a desk-written claim would look like. I filtered the whole sprint-12 diff of that file for any added or removed line that is not a comment: EMPTY. Every one of those 62 lines is comment. The template text is byte-identical to what shipped in 0.1.11. The claim is true and it is the kind of claim that would have been trivial to get wrong.

That matters more than it sounds. In sprint 11 the provenance comment claimed a six-role two-gate pass that the handoff contradicted. Here the analogous claim is independently verifiable from the repository and it verifies.

INTERNAL CONSISTENCY OF THE RUN LOG. Seven invocations with per-role cost, turn count and is_error status, totalling ~$4.78. Cross-checked the details that could be wrong and are not: Pipeman "correctly determined this scratch repo has no package.json (so no release, no npm step)" is consistent with how install.js actually behaves — package.json is not in FRAMEWORK_OWNED and is never copied into a target, so a scratch install genuinely has none. Master Controller "explicitly declined to amend the sprint file (would invalidate QA1's audited-file hash)" is the correct behaviour under this framework's own hash gate. LiveQA "correctly identified there is no deployed product to browser-test" and recorded a scoped PASS rather than fabricating a browser session or refusing — which is the exact judgement call this project has needed from that role for ten sprints. None of that reads as invented, and the specific details are ones an invented log would get wrong.

REQ 5 — THE FINDING IS STATED, AS THE CRITERION UNUSUALLY REQUIRED. "The templates themselves needed no changes... The desk design survived contact." That is exactly the explicit statement the criterion asked for rather than a silent non-event, and I verified it independently above rather than accepting it. Worth saying plainly: sprint 11's design, built from the sprint file's own guidance and shipped labelled as unvalidated, turned out to be right. Labelling it provisional was still correct — it was unvalidated at the time — and this is what validating it looks like.

REQ 6 — MET. Ran every template through a restated-state check. Five came back clean. Pipeman's flagged on my own crude filter because its pointer contains the string "PASS" — but the text is "Point: the state file's most recent QA1 PASS entry and the commit it recorded as audited," which names what to look for and does not restate any verdict. That is pointing, not summarizing, and it is the same text I cleared in sprint 11. A false positive of my filter, not a finding, and I am recording it as such rather than as a catch.

REQ 1 / REQ 3 IMPLEMENTATION — MET. The shipped HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES match the recorded decision role by role: `acceptEdits` for everyone, per-role `--allowedTools` naming specific script invocations rather than categories, `--disallowedTools "Edit,Write"` for qa1 and liveqa. headlessPermissionArgs throws loudly if a role is added without a profile rather than launching unscoped, which is the right failure direction. Pipeman gets `Bash(npm *)` and nobody else does.

REQ 8 — MET. Ran it: 123 OK lines, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED.
verify-tarball.sh: TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, sprint data clean.

THE --notes-file FIX IS GOOD, AND IT CAME FROM THE RIGHT PLACE. Three roles independently flagging the same gap, unprompted, is real evidence rather than one role's phrasing. The quoted-heredoc alternative preserves the exact property the Write-tool pattern existed for — no expansion, no substitution — and it is correctly ranked above the "confirm your notes are clean and inline them" fallback, which only covers the case where they happen to be clean. Confirmed by a real run. This closes a gap my own gate created in sprint 11.

================================================================
FINDING 1 (blocking) — REQ 7 IS NOT MET, AND IT BLOCKS THE LIVE GATE
================================================================

package.json is 0.1.11. Req 7's criterion is "package.json is 0.1.12, one-line diff." Unlike sprint 11, this sprint's Dependencies contain no hold clause — I grepped for one. The bump is simply not done, and the tarball confirms it: verify-tarball installs "0.1.11 (first install)".

This is the same sequencing trap I raised in sprint 11 round 5, and passing it here would be both inconsistent and more expensive:
  - A PASS records this tree's hash. A later bump changes package.json, changes the tree, and
    /sprint-ship refuses with no override. The re-audit happens anyway, after a confused Pipeman.
  - If nobody bumps: pipeman.md's trigger is "package.json changed since the last ship." 0.1.11 is
    live on the registry (checked: `npm view` returns 0.1.11, and sprint 11's last_shipped_commit is
    8606700). package.json has not changed since. The publish step is never reached, nothing goes to
    the registry, and LiveQA's first criterion — "Confirm 0.1.12 is on the registry" — is unreachable.
    The entire live gate stalls, including the three criteria carried here specifically because this
    sprint is what unblocks them.
  - Had it been reached, npm would reject a duplicate 0.1.11 outright.

One line, and the whole gate-2 sequence depends on it.

================================================================
FINDING 2 (blocking, and it is the security-shaped one) — "WRITES NOTHING" IS NOT WHAT THE PROFILE ACTUALLY GUARANTEES
================================================================

The findings document characterizes QA1's profile as "QA1 (runs tests and reads code, **writes nothing**)". The same sprint, in the same merge, ships instructions in `.claude/agents/qa1.md` and `liveqa.md` telling exactly those two roles how to write a file headless:

    cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/qa1-notes-<N>.txt ... EOF

and states it was "confirmed by an actual headless run recording real notes this way and reading them back out of the state file intact." So by this sprint's own evidence, a role whose profile is described as writing nothing can write files. The two artifacts prove each other's point; I do not have to speculate.

To be precise about what is and is not wrong here, because the mechanism is fine and the description is not:
  - `--disallowedTools "Edit,Write"` does what the document says: those TOOLS are hard-disabled. That
    finding is correct.
  - What it does not do is prevent writing. Bash redirection under `acceptEdits` writes files, and
    qa1's allowlist does not need to name `cat` for it — `acceptEdits` auto-approves that command
    category on its own, which is why the documented workaround works at all.
  - There is also an unremarked asymmetry in the document's own evidence: the Write TOOL was observed
    BLOCKED writing to an absolute /tmp path outside the working directory ("acceptEdits's
    auto-approval appears to already be confined to the launch working directory"), while the heredoc
    demonstrably wrote to /tmp successfully. So the directory confinement the document offers as a
    reassuring free bound applies to one write path and not the other. That is worth knowing before
    anyone relies on it.

Why this is blocking rather than a note: Req 3's recorded decision is the thing LiveQA is about to verify ("confirm it is genuinely constrained rather than nominally so"), and the sprint's own summary line overstates the constraint. A reader deciding whether the residual risk is acceptable — which Req 3 explicitly leaves to the user — would be deciding on a description that is stronger than the mechanism. That is the same class as sprint 11's provenance comment, which this team fixed properly, and it deserves the same treatment.

REQUIRED FIX: correct the characterization, not necessarily the profile. Say what is true — Edit/Write are hard-disabled so the role cannot edit source through the normal path, while Bash-mediated writes remain possible under acceptEdits and are in fact the documented way these roles record their notes — and note the confinement asymmetry. Whether to tighten the scope further is a decision on this evidence and is the user's under Req 3, not mine and not a thing to change quietly here.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL — NOT REQUIRED FIXES
================================================================

1. The npm publish paragraph ends "the corrected version published clean on retry." In context this is plainly still the `--dry-run` (the paragraph opens by naming it), but read alone that sentence describes a real publish. One word — "dry-ran clean" — removes the ambiguity in a document whose whole purpose is that claims match what happened.
2. The findings document is the best artifact this project has produced and should not be left as a loose file in `docs/`. It is the reference Req 3's decision cites and the input to any future scope question; it is worth a line in README's structure section so it is findable by someone who was not here.
3. Carried, unchanged: the `--agents` argv budget against Windows' 32,767-char limit; the interactive auth-check ordering from sprint 11 round 1; and sprint 10's structural gitHead gap, which the sprint 13 amendment at 5124156 suggests is now being tracked properly.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================

Two fixes, one commit: bump package.json to 0.1.12, and correct the "writes nothing" characterization in the findings document (and anywhere the per-role summary repeats it). Then round 2, which will be short — I have no other open items and the code is otherwise sound.

Then /sprint-dev-done 12, and Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.12. Publish from a detached checkout of the audited commit so gitHead is the audited commit by construction — two releases have now needed a post-hoc correction for want of it.

Last thing, and it is not a finding: this sprint fixed a gap my own gate created. Sprint 11's Req 7, which I passed, mandated a Write-tool pattern that sprint 12's own permission profile then made impossible for the two roles it was written for. Three headless roles found it independently and none of them worked around it unsafely. That is the framework catching its own instruction, which is what all of this is for.

PASS: PASS — round 2. Audited c50530c (bookkeeping) on 6adc44b (the fix), main checkout. Sprint file re-read fresh; `git diff abf97e2 HEAD -- docs/sprints/2-in-progress/` is empty, so the requirements are byte-identical to round 1's. Code untouched: `git diff abf97e2 HEAD -- scripts/` is empty.

Both findings closed. One of them was closed better than I asked for, and the way it was closed is the most valuable thing in this round.

================================================================
FINDING 1 — CLOSED
================================================================

package.json is 0.1.12. verify-tarball.sh packs and installs it: "Installed 0.1.12 (first install)", TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, docs/sprints clean, baseline table present with 7 paths. The registry was checked before bumping (0.1.11 live, no hold clause in this sprint), which is the right order.

================================================================
FINDING 2 — CLOSED BY TESTING, NOT BY REWORDING, AND IT FOUND MORE THAN I DID
================================================================

I asked for the characterization to be corrected. What came back is three separate results, each run rather than argued:

  1. The correction itself is right. "--disallowedTools 'Edit,Write' — CONFIRMED to hard-disable the
     TOOLS, not to prevent all writes," with the contradiction named explicitly: one artifact said
     "writes nothing," the other gave instructions for writing a file. The per-role summary line is
     corrected too, not just the section heading.

  2. MY FLAGGED ASYMMETRY WAS WRONG, AND THEY PROVED IT RATHER THAN ACCEPTING IT. I hypothesized that
     the working-directory bound applied to the Write tool but not to Bash redirection, on the evidence
     that a heredoc had reached /tmp. Tested directly: `printf ... > /tmp/outside-file.txt` from a
     different working directory is blocked with "Output redirection to '/tmp/...' was blocked. For
     security, Claude Code may only write to files in the allowed working directories for this
     session." The bound is symmetric, enforced at the Bash-redirect level too. My hypothesis was the
     wrong explanation for the observation, and the right response was to run it rather than write
     around it. Gap closed, and closed in the direction that makes the mechanism stronger than I
     credited.

  3. THE THIRD THING, WHICH NEITHER OF US HAD: heredocs are rejected outright under this profile —
     "Contains shell syntax (file_redirect) that cannot be statically analyzed" — regardless of
     location, a stricter and different block from the directory bound. Which means the fallback that
     SHIPPED in round 1, in four files, never worked as written.

I verified the replacement independently rather than taking the od -c claim on trust. Ran the recommended form myself with adversarial content:
    printf '%s\n' 'a backtick `whoami` here' 'a dollar $HOME here' 'a backslash \n literal' > file
    od -c shows real \n bytes at the line boundaries — genuine newlines, not literal backslash-n.
    The backtick survives as a literal backtick; `$HOME` survives as literal `$HOME`. Nothing expanded,
    nothing substituted.
That is exactly the property the original --notes-file mandate exists to protect, delivered by a command shape that actually executes under this profile. The claim holds.

All four files are corrected — qa1.md, liveqa.md, sprint-qa1.md, sprint-liveqa.md — and each one names the failed form explicitly ("Do not use a heredoc... it was documented here once and didn't work") rather than quietly swapping it. Naming the retracted instruction is what stops someone rediscovering it from an old transcript.

================================================================
WORTH RECORDING PLAINLY: A "CONFIRMED BY RUNNING" CLAIM WAS WRONG, AND DEV TEAM CAUGHT IT, NOT ME
================================================================

Round 1's document said the heredoc fallback was "confirmed by an actual headless run recording real notes this way and reading them back out of the state file intact." Round 2 establishes that heredocs cannot execute under this profile at all. Those cannot both be true, and the round-1 claim was false.

I did not catch it. I read that sentence in round 1, treated CONFIRMED as CONFIRMED, and passed over it — my Finding 2 was about the characterization being too strong, not about the fallback being non-functional. Dev Team found it by testing the thing I flagged for a different reason.

This is not a defect to record against this round; it is the correction, and self-correction on evidence is precisely what the grading system exists to produce. But it is worth being honest about what it means: a CONFIRMED label is only as good as the run behind it, and this project has now produced one that was not. The grading discipline still works — it worked here, one round later, from the inside. It is not a substitute for the thing being re-run when something adjacent to it turns out to be wrong.

RESIDUAL, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING I FOUND — INFORMATIONAL, NOT BLOCKING. The findings document's own "three roles independently hit the same tooling gap" section (line ~229) still reads "All three found working, safe alternatives on their own (a quoted heredoc via Bash; ...)". That now contradicts the corrected section at line 81 and the four corrected files. One sentence, in the historical narrative rather than in any operative instruction, in a document that is the reference Req 3's decision cites. Fix it whenever that file is next open — say the roles PROPOSED a heredoc and that it was subsequently found not to execute, which is both true and a better story than the current one. Not blocking: every instruction anyone would actually follow is correct and verified.

================================================================
REPORTING ACCURACY — NO VERDICT IMPACT, RECORDED BECAUSE IT KEEPS HAPPENING
================================================================

The handoff says "116/116". It is 123/123, and the test file is untouched this round (`git diff abf97e2 HEAD -- scripts/` is empty), so nothing was removed — 116 is sprint 11's number, carried forward. I counted ^OK lines and ran the suite: 123, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED.

Sixth reporting item across twelve sprints, and the pattern has not changed once: it has never been the code that was wrong, only the number describing it. Harmless here precisely because I ran the suite instead of believing the handoff — which is the only reason it has been harmless every previous time too.

================================================================
EVERYTHING ELSE FROM ROUND 1 STANDS
================================================================

Not re-derived: Req 2's grading (no unrun scope claimed as working), Req 3's implementation (no bypassPermissions anywhere outside a test asserting its absence; per-role profiles matching the recorded decision), the npm publish --dry-run evidence, Req 4's discovery pass and its internal consistency, Req 5's stated finding that the desk design survived contact (which I verified independently — prompts.js's non-comment diff is empty), Req 6's templates carrying no restated state, Req 8's suite.

INFORMATIONAL, CARRIED

1. docs/sprint-12-permission-scope-findings.md is still a loose file in docs/. It is the reference Req 3's decision cites and the input to any future scope question. Worth a line in README's structure section.
2. The npm publish paragraph still ends "the corrected version published clean on retry" — in context plainly the dry-run, but "dry-ran clean" removes the ambiguity.
3. docs/sprints/registry.json is modified and uncommitted in the main checkout, and there is an untracked sprint-14 file. Neither is in this sprint's diff; flagging so whoever commits next knows what is sitting there.
4. Carried: the --agents argv budget against Windows' 32,767-char limit; the interactive auth-check ordering from sprint 11 round 1.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 12, then Pipeman ships --commit c50530c specifically — this PASS records that commit's tree (e288b0cd1014ec47da145ac52eeae66a8a14a6d9), and if bookkeeping lands on top first, /sprint-ship will refuse.

Publish from a detached checkout of the audited commit so gitHead is the audited commit by construction. Sprint 10's release needed a post-hoc correction for want of that, sprint 13's amendment at 5124156 suggests worktree-published releases lost gitHead entirely, and this is the third release in a row where it matters.

Then LiveQA runs the six-role pass against a published 0.1.12 — including the three criteria carried here that sprint 11 could not demonstrate, which this sprint's scoped profile is what unblocks.

CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.1.12 with a real headless role launch against the live registry. Environment: macOS Darwin arm64, claude 2.1.259, scratch git repo /tmp/fc12, 2026-09-03.

The scoped profile works and the carried-over exit-code criterion passes. The conditional is on shipped instructions that the shipped profile denies — demonstrated, with the exact denied command. Several criteria are outstanding and are listed plainly at the end rather than inferred.

PROVENANCE — VERIFIED, AND SPRINT 11's REGRESSION IS FIXED
`npm view fully-completely version` -> 0.1.12; dist-tags latest -> 0.1.12; `npm view fully-completely@0.1.12 gitHead` -> c50530cac0e74d720f71cdb494ae0feed1509a1e, an exact match for last_shipped_commit. `git rev-parse c50530c^{tree}` = e288b0cd1014ec47da145ac52eeae66a8a14a6d9, identical to the recorded qa1_audited_tree_hash. Remote tag v0.1.12 dereferences to the same commit.

The gitHead field is back. Sprint 11 published from a linked worktree and npm silently omitted gitHead entirely, forcing me to substitute a 55-file content comparison. Publishing from a real `git clone` this round restored it, so the registry once again carries its own independent attestation. Pipeman's root cause and correction were both right.

Registry propagation was slow, as flagged: my first `npx -y fully-completely@0.1.12` exceeded 120 seconds and had to be re-run with a longer window before it completed. Consistent with the ~24 minute publish-to-queryable lag reported; not a defect, recorded so the next tester does not mistake it for a broken package.

================================================================
CRITERION — 0.1.12 ON THE REGISTRY WITH MATCHING gitHead: PASS. Covered above.
================================================================

================================================================
CRITERION — "A RECORDED FAIL EXITS 0": PASS. CARRIED FROM SPRINT 11, NOW DEMONSTRATED.
================================================================
This is the criterion sprint 11 could not reach: there, the role composed a full QA1 FAIL verdict and was denied the Write that persists it, so the exit-code property was never exercised.

From a published 0.1.12 install in a scratch git repo, with a throwaway sprint at dev_build:
  node scripts/launcher/run-role.js --headless --agent qa1 --sprint 1 </dev/null

Completed in ~120s. EXIT CODE 0. 8,363 bytes of strictly parseable JSON on stdout, ZERO bytes on stderr. Envelope: is_error false, subtype "success", num_turns 18, total_cost_usd 1.034292.

And the verdict genuinely landed, checked in the state machine rather than inferred from the envelope:
  Sprint 1: Headless gate probe
  Phase: dev_build
  QA1 audit result: FAIL (rounds: 1)
The recorded notes are 2,767 characters of real audit content, not a truncated stub — I read them out of the state file to confirm. The sprint was correctly returned to dev_build by the FAIL.

So: a role recorded a FAIL, the sprint moved as a FAIL should, and the process exited 0. A negative verdict does not read as a broken harness. Sprint 12's scoped profile is exactly what unblocked this, as the sprint file predicted.

================================================================
CRITERION — THE PERMISSION SCOPE HOLDS IN PRACTICE: PASS, AND IT IS GENUINELY CONSTRAINED
================================================================
The sprint asks specifically whether scoping is real or nominal. It is real, and I have three denials to prove it rather than an absence of evidence.

The run's `permission_denials` array carries three blocked Bash calls, all of them things qa1's profile does not allow:
  1. `ls templates/ && echo "=== DIFF: ..." && for f in tem...`  — exploratory compound command
  2. `echo "=== DEMO 1: diff template vs sprint file ..." && diff templates/sprin...`  — exploratory compound command
  3. the notes-file write, discussed below
qa1's profile is `disallowedTools: ['Edit','Write']` plus an allowlist of specific `Bash(...)` patterns. Both Edit and Write were unavailable to it for the whole run and it never obtained them. The role nonetheless completed its audit and recorded a verdict. That is a genuinely constrained agent doing its job, not a bypass wearing a scope's clothing.

================================================================
FINDING (blocking this round) — THE SHIPPED INSTRUCTIONS TELL ROLES TO WRITE SOMEWHERE THE SHIPPED PROFILE BLOCKS
================================================================
Sprint 12 replaced the heredoc guidance with a `printf` pattern after the heredoc was found to fail. The replacement was written into three shipped files. The role followed it exactly, and it was DENIED.

The denied command, extracted verbatim from the envelope's permission_denials, ends:
  ... "They were handed an empty spec." > /tmp/qa1-notes-1.txt

That redirect target is precisely what `.claude/agents/qa1.md` instructs:
  "use `printf` via Bash instead of a heredoc: `printf '%s\n' "line one" "line two" ... > /tmp/qa1-notes-<N>.txt`"

The same sentence in the same file already contains the reason it cannot work:
  "though a plain Bash redirect still works, CONFINED TO YOUR WORKING DIRECTORY"

/tmp is not the working directory. And run-role.js's own comment at :246-247 records the governing fact independently: `--permission-mode acceptEdits` auto-approves writes WITHIN the launch directory, and "a write outside it, to an absolute /tmp path, was still blocked under acceptEdits". So the constraint was known, written down in the launcher, and the instruction shipped pointing outside it anyway.

Affected files, all three carrying the same absolute-/tmp path:
  .claude/agents/qa1.md
  .claude/agents/liveqa.md
  .claude/commands/sprint-liveqa.md   ("Headless note (sprint 12)")

WHY THIS IS A CONDITIONAL AND NOT A FAIL. The outcome was correct: the role adapted after the denial and recorded its full 2,767-character notes, and the run exited 0. Nothing was lost and no criterion outcome was changed. The gate works.

WHY IT IS STILL BLOCKING. Sprint 12's whole deliverable is settling the permission scope and writing down how roles operate inside it. Shipping a documented procedure that the profile denies on first use is that deliverable being wrong in the specific place it is supposed to be right. Three consequences:
 - It costs a turn and a retry on every headless role run that follows the instruction as written.
 - Recovery depends on the agent improvising a workaround. This framework's consumer is an unattended orchestrator; a less capable model, or a stricter future profile, does not necessarily recover, and the failure mode is a verdict that never gets recorded — the exact thing sprint 11 hit.
 - It is the same defect class QA1 already flagged in docs/sprint-12-permission-scope-findings.md, where a "found working" claim survives next to the corrected section that contradicts it. The prose got corrected; the path in the instruction did not.

REQUIRED FIX: point the notes path at the working directory rather than /tmp in all three files — the instruction's own parenthetical already states the correct rule, so this is making the example agree with the sentence around it. Wording and exact path are Dev Team's. What must be true afterwards is that a headless role following the shipped instruction verbatim writes its notes file without a permission denial. Worth fixing the findings-doc contradiction in the same pass, since that file is now being touched for a real reason.

================================================================
NOT DEMONSTRATED THIS ROUND — STATED PLAINLY, NOT INFERRED
================================================================
I recorded this verdict as soon as the finding above was confirmed rather than holding it behind the remaining work, because none of the outstanding items can change it: the shipped instruction is denied whatever they show. They remain genuinely outstanding and should be covered in round 2, when the fix reships.

 1. THE SIX-ROLE END-TO-END RUN. The criterion is to launch each of the six roles headless and drive one throwaway sprint through both gates. I launched ONE role (qa1) and drove the sprint to a recorded FAIL. master-controller, dev-team-1, dev-team-2, pipeman and liveqa were not launched, and the sprint was not driven through to completion. This is the sprint's central deliverable and it is only partly exercised. Cost is the honest reason as much as the finding: the single qa1 run billed $1.03, so a full six-role pass is a meaningful spend on the user's account, and I stopped once the verdict was determined rather than spend it to confirm a conclusion already reached.

 2. THE INTERACTIVE PATH AS A REAL GUI RUN, ON macOS AND WINDOWS. Requires a VS Code window and seven visible terminals on two platforms. Not attempted this round. Sprint 11's content-level no-regression evidence still stands and is not a substitute; the criterion explicitly says so.

 3. THE ORPHANED-CHILD BEHAVIOUR UNDER THE SCOPED PROFILE. Sprint 11 established that killing the launcher leaves the spawned claude alive, reparented to PPID 1 and still billing. The criterion asks what happens under the scoped profile. My 0.1.12 run completed normally and was never killed, so I did not exercise it and have nothing to report. Unchanged from sprint 11 as far as I know, which is not the same as verified.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
Everything above I ran and observed directly on macOS against the live registry and a real published install. The denied command was read out of the run's own envelope, and the recorded verdict was confirmed by querying the state machine, not by trusting the agent's own summary of what it had done. Pipeman's gitHead claim was verified against the registry and against the audited tree hash; the propagation-lag warning was borne out by my own timed-out first install.

I did not treat QA1's advance note about the findings-doc contradiction as covering this: that note is about a stale sentence in a docs file, and what I found is the operative instruction in three shipped files being denied in practice.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Fix the notes path in the three files so it lands inside the working directory, correct the findings-doc contradiction while that file is open, reship, and I will re-test. The fix is small and the sprint's substance is sound — the scoped profile is genuinely constraining, a headless role completes real work under it, and a recorded FAIL exits 0, which is the property sprint 11 could not reach and the one that most needed proving.

Round 2 should also cover what this round did not: the full six-role pass through both gates, the interactive path as a GUI run on both platforms, and the orphan behaviour under a killed launcher. I would rather those be run against the corrected instruction anyway, since a six-role pass on the current build would be measuring how well each role improvises around a denial rather than whether the documented path works.

This CONDITIONAL means the code is close, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 12.
